title: Βρισηΐς
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The ship bearing Chryseis sails on, while the army purifies itself and offers Apollo a hecatomb on the shore. Agamemnon, who has not dropped his quarrel with Achilles, sends the heralds Talthybius and Eurybates to take Briseis from him by the hand, and warns that he will come himself with more men if she is not given. The heralds go unwillingly and stand in awe and silence before Achilles, who greets them kindly, blames only Agamemnon, has Patroclus bring the girl out, and calls the heralds, the gods and Agamemnon himself to witness, should the Achaeans ever need him again to ward off ruin, a threat he leaves unfinished. Briseis goes with the heralds against her will, and Achilles, weeping, withdraws alone to the shore of the grey sea and prays to his mother. Thetis rises from the sea like a mist and asks what grieves him. He tells her the whole story, from the taking of Thebe and the coming of Chryses to the plague and the quarrel, and bids her go to Olympus, remind Zeus how she once freed him from the gods who wished to bind him, and beg him to help the Trojans and hem the Achaeans in at their ships until Agamemnon learns what it is to have dishonoured the best of them.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἀναβάντες ἐπέπλεον ὑγρὰ κέλευθα,
λαοὺς δ’ Ἀτρεΐδης ἀπολυμαίνεσθαι ἄνωγεν·
sentences.tr:
hoi men epeit’ anabantes epepleon hygra keleutha,
laous d’ Atreïdēs apolymainesthai anōgen·
sentences.l:
They then, having embarked, sailed over the watery ways,
while the people Atreus’-son ordered to purify themselves;
sentences.i: Then they embarked and sailed over the watery ways, while the son of Atreus ordered the people to purify themselves;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν are the party aboard the ship launched at 308–311: Odysseus, the twenty oarsmen and Chryseis. ἀναβάντες is ‘having gone up’, that is on board, and ἐπέπλεον ‘sailed over’ (an imperfect). The line is Odyssey 15.474 word for word, apart from the accent on οἳ, and keeps its English; its second half is also Odyssey 4.842. ὑγρὰ κέλευθα is ‘the watery ways’ (ὑγρός ‘wet’, κέλευθα ‘paths’). ἀπολυμαίνεσθαι is ‘to cleanse oneself’, to wash off a defilement (compare λύματα in the next line); λαούς is the whole army, and Ἀτρεΐδης, ‘Atreus’-son’, is Agamemnon.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀπελυμαίνοντο καὶ εἰς ἅλα λύματα βάλλον,
ἕρδον δ’ Ἀπόλλωνι τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας
ταύρων ἠδ’ αἰγῶν παρὰ θῖν’ ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ apelymainonto kai eis hala lymata ballon,
herdon d’ Apollōni telēessas hekatombas
taurōn ēd’ aigōn para thin’ halos atrygetoio·
sentences.i: and they purified themselves and threw the filth into the sea, and offered Apollo complete hecatombs of bulls and goats along the shore of the sea that yields no harvest;
sentences.n: ἀπελυμαίνοντο and ἕρδον are imperfects, ‘were cleansing themselves’ and ‘were offering’: the army does these things while the ship is under way. λύματα is the filth washed off, thrown into the sea. ἕρδω is ‘do’, and with a sacrifice ‘offer’. τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας keeps the Odyssey’s ‘complete hecatombs’; a ἑκατόμβη is a great sacrifice and need not be a hundred beasts, and here the victims are bulls and goats. ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο is the Odyssey’s formula, ‘of the unharvested salt-sea’, in English ‘of the sea that yields no harvest’; what ἀτρύγετος means is not known, and that is only the usual guess. θῖν’ is θῖνα ‘shore’, elided.

sentences.t: κνίση δ’ οὐρανὸν ἷκεν ἑλισσομένη περὶ καπνῷ.
sentences.tr: knisē d’ ouranon hiken helissomenē peri kapnōi.
sentences.l: and the savour reached heaven, curling about in the smoke.
sentences.i: And the savour of it reached heaven, curling about in the smoke.
sentences.n: κνίση is the savour of burning fat, the part of a sacrifice that rises to the gods. οὐρανόν is ‘heaven, the sky’ and ἷκεν ‘reached’, the unaugmented past tense of ἵκω ‘come to’. ἑλισσομένη is the participle of ἑλίσσομαι ‘turn, wind, curl’, agreeing with κνίση; περὶ καπνῷ, ‘about the smoke’, puts the savour curling round in it.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν τὰ πένοντο κατὰ στρατόν·
sentences.tr: hōs hoi men ta penonto kata straton·
sentences.l: So they, then, were busied with these things throughout the army;
sentences.i: So they busied themselves with these tasks throughout the army;
sentences.n: ὣς οἳ μὲν closes the scene at the shore and sets up the contrast with Agamemnon in the next clause. τά is the article used as a pronoun, ‘these things’; πένοντο is the imperfect middle of πένομαι ‘be busied with’ (the Odyssey’s verb for busying oneself with a meal). κατὰ στρατόν is ‘throughout the army’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ Ἀγαμέμνων
λῆγ’ ἔριδος τὴν πρῶτον ἐπηπείλησ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε Ταλθύβιόν τε καὶ Εὐρυβάτην προσέειπε,
τώ οἱ ἔσαν κήρυκε καὶ ὀτρηρὼ θεράποντε·
sentences.tr:
oud’ Agamemnōn
lēg’ eridos tēn prōton epēpeilēs’ Achilēï,
all’ ho ge Talthybion te kai Eurybatēn proseeipe,
tō hoi esan kēryke kai otrērō theraponte·
sentences.l:
nor did Agamemnon
cease from the strife which at first he threatened to Achilles,
but he addressed Talthybius and Eurybates,
the two who were his heralds and brisk attendants:
sentences.i: Nor did Agamemnon give up the strife with which he had first threatened Achilles; he addressed Talthybius and Eurybates, the two who were his heralds and brisk attendants:
sentences.n: λῆγ’ is λῆγε, the imperfect of λήγω ‘cease from’, unaugmented and with the genitive ἔριδος ‘strife’ (compare λῆγ’ ἔριδος at 210, where it is an imperative). τὴν is the relative ‘which’, the strife Agamemnon threatened at the assembly. προσέειπε is the epic aorist ‘addressed’. τώ is the dual of the article used as a relative, ‘the two who’; κήρυκε and ὀτρηρὼ θεράποντε are dual too, and ὀτρηρὸς θεράπων keeps the Odyssey’s ‘brisk attendant’. ἔσαν is ἦσαν ‘were’, and οἱ ‘to him’ stands for ‘his’.

sentences.t: ἔρχεσθον κλισίην Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος·
sentences.tr: erchesthon klisiēn Pēlēïadeō Achilēos·
sentences.l: “Go, you two, to the hut of Peleus’-son Achilles;
sentences.i: “Go, you two, to the hut of Achilles, son of Peleus;
sentences.n: ἔρχεσθον is the dual imperative, ‘go, you two’, to the heralds. The dual number, for exactly two, is regular in this scene. κλισίην is an accusative of goal, ‘to the hut’, without a preposition. Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος is the patronymic with the epic genitive -εω, ‘Peleus’-son’, as in the poem’s first line.

sentences.t: χειρὸς ἑλόντ’ ἀγέμεν Βρισηΐδα καλλιπάρῃον·
sentences.tr: cheiros helont’ agemen Brisēïda kalliparēion·
sentences.l: by the hand taking (her), lead Briseis, fair-cheeked;
sentences.i: take Briseis, fair-cheeked, by the hand and lead her away;
sentences.n: χειρὸς ἑλόντ’ is the dual aorist participle of αἱρέω, ‘taking by the hand’, with the genitive of the part grasped; the Greek gives no object, and Βρισηΐδα comes with the next verb. ἀγέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἄγω ‘lead’, used as an imperative. καλλιπάρῃον ‘fair-cheeked’ is the epithet already given to Chryseis at 1.143.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κε μὴ δώῃσιν ἐγὼ δέ κεν αὐτὸς ἕλωμαι
ἐλθὼν σὺν πλεόνεσσι·
sentences.tr:
ei de ke mē dōēisin egō de ken autos helōmai
elthōn syn pleonessi·
sentences.l:
but if he does not give, I myself shall take,
coming with more men;
sentences.i: but if he does not give her up, I shall come myself with more men and take her;
sentences.n: εἰ … μὴ δώῃσιν is ‘if he does not give’, the aorist subjunctive with κε; the object ‘her’ is understood. The edition prints no stop after δώῃσιν. The δέ in ἐγὼ δέ κεν opens the main clause, ‘then I’, and κε ἕλωμαι is a subjunctive standing for a future, ‘I shall take’. πλεόνεσσι is πλείοσι ‘more’; the Greek names no one, so ‘men’ is supplied, and it means more than two heralds.

sentences.t: τό οἱ καὶ ῥίγιον ἔσται.
sentences.tr: to hoi kai rhigion estai.
sentences.l: that for him will be even worse.”
sentences.i: and that will be the worse for him.”
sentences.n: τό is ‘that’, the seizure of the girl by force with an armed party. οἱ is ‘for him’, Achilles. ῥίγιον is a comparative, ‘worse, harder to bear’, probably related to ῥῖγος ‘chill, shudder’; καὶ is ‘even’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν προΐει, κρατερὸν δ’ ἐπὶ μῦθον ἔτελλε·
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn proïei, krateron d’ epi mython etelle·
sentences.l: So having spoken he sent them forth, and a strong word enjoined on them;
sentences.i: So saying, he sent them forth and laid a strong charge on them.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’. προΐει is the imperfect of προΐημι ‘send forth’. κρατερὸν δ’ ἐπὶ μῦθον ἔτελλε is the formula of 1.25, in the same English: ἐπὶ … ἔτελλε is a tmesis, ‘enjoined on’, and κρατερός keeps ‘strong’. The charge has just been given, so the line only seals it; the same formula comes again at 379.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἀέκοντε βάτην παρὰ θῖν’ ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο,
Μυρμιδόνων δ’ ἐπί τε κλισίας καὶ νῆας ἱκέσθην,
τὸν δ’ εὗρον παρά τε κλισίῃ καὶ νηῒ μελαίνῃ
ἥμενον·
sentences.tr:
tō d’ aekonte batēn para thin’ halos atrygetoio,
Myrmidonōn d’ epi te klisias kai nēas hikesthēn,
ton d’ heuron para te klisiēi kai nēï melainēi
hēmenon·
sentences.l:
And the two, unwilling, went along the shore of the unharvested salt-sea,
and to the huts and the ships of the Myrmidons they came,
and him they found beside hut and black ship
sitting;
sentences.i: The two went unwilling along the shore of the sea that yields no harvest, and came to the huts and ships of the Myrmidons, and found him sitting beside his hut and his black ship.
sentences.n: τὼ is the dual article, ‘the two’; βάτην is the dual of the unaugmented aorist ἔβην ‘went’, and ἱκέσθην the dual of ἱκόμην ‘came’. ἀέκοντε ‘unwilling’ is dual as well, the Odyssey’s ἀέκων. εὗρον is plural although the subject is still the pair, which Homer allows. The shore phrase is the one of 316, and the Myrmidons are Achilles’ men, their name in the genitive depending on both κλισίας and νῆας. νηῒ μελαίνῃ ‘black ship’ is printed with a diaeresis. ἥμενον ‘sitting’ agrees with τόν, Achilles.

sentences.t: οὐδ’ ἄρα τώ γε ἰδὼν γήθησεν Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr: oud’ ara tō ge idōn gēthēsen Achilleus.
sentences.l: And Achilles, seeing those two, did not then rejoice.
sentences.i: Achilles did not rejoice to see them.
sentences.n: τώ γε is the dual ‘those two’, with γε stressing them; ἰδών ‘seeing’. ἄρα marks what is to be expected: the two come on Agamemnon’s errand. γήθησεν is the aorist of γηθέω ‘rejoice’, with the same English as in the Odyssey.

sentences.t:
τὼ μὲν ταρβήσαντε καὶ αἰδομένω βασιλῆα
στήτην, οὐδέ τί μιν προσεφώνεον οὐδ’ ἐρέοντο·
sentences.tr:
tō men tarbēsante kai aidomenō basilēa
stētēn, oude ti min prosephōneon oud’ ereonto·
sentences.l:
And the two, frightened and in awe of the king,
stood, and not a word to him did they speak, nor ask him anything;
sentences.i: The two stood there, frightened and in awe of the king, and did not say a word to him or ask him anything;
sentences.n: τὼ μέν points the contrast with αὐτὰρ ὅ of the next line. ταρβήσαντε is the dual aorist participle of ταρβέω ‘be frightened’, and αἰδομένω the dual present participle of αἰδέομαι ‘stand in awe of’; the king, βασιλῆα, is Achilles here, though at 340 the same word will mean Agamemnon. στήτην is the dual of ἔστην ‘stood’. προσεφώνεον and ἐρέοντο are plural verbs with a dual subject; ἐρέοντο is from ἐρέομαι, the epic form of ἔρομαι ‘ask’, and προσεφώνεον is ‘spoke to’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ ἔγνω ᾗσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: autar ho egnō hēisin eni phresi phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: But he knew in his own wits, and spoke:
sentences.i: But he understood in his own mind, and spoke:
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ is ‘but he’, Achilles. ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘know, recognise’, and the Greek gives it no object; the speech that follows shows he has read their silence. ᾗσιν is the possessive ‘his own’ (= ἑῇσιν), not a relative, and φρεσί ‘in the wits’ is the dative plural of φρήν with ἐνί for ἐν. φώνησεν is ‘lifted his voice, spoke’, and the enclitic τε joins it to ἔγνω.

sentences.t:
χαίρετε κήρυκες Διὸς ἄγγελοι ἠδὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν,
ἆσσον ἴτ’·
sentences.tr:
chairete kērykes Dios angeloi ēde kai andrōn,
asson it’·
sentences.l:
“Welcome, heralds, messengers of Zeus and also of men,
come nearer;
sentences.i: “Welcome, heralds, messengers of Zeus and of men as well; come nearer;
sentences.n: χαίρετε is the plural of χαῖρε, the greeting that the Odyssey table renders ‘Welcome’. κήρυκες Διὸς ἄγγελοι ἠδὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν says that heralds carry messages between gods and men, which is why he treats them as persons not to be blamed. ἆσσον is the comparative adverb ‘nearer’, and ἴτ’ is ἴτε, the plural imperative of εἶμι. Achilles speaks to them in the plural here and in ὔμμες of the next line, and in the dual when he speaks of them as a pair (σφῶϊ at 336, σφωϊν and ἔστων at 338).

sentences.t:
οὔ τί μοι ὔμμες ἐπαίτιοι ἀλλ’ Ἀγαμέμνων,
ὃ σφῶϊ προΐει Βρισηΐδος εἵνεκα κούρης.
sentences.tr:
ou ti moi ymmes epaitioi all’ Agamemnōn,
ho sphōï proïei Brisēïdos heineka kourēs.
sentences.l:
not at all to me are you to blame, but Agamemnon,
who sent you two forth for the sake of the girl Briseis.
sentences.i: It is not you who are to blame, in my eyes, but Agamemnon, who sent you forth for the sake of the girl Briseis.
sentences.n: ὔμμες is the Aeolic plural ‘you’ (= ὑμεῖς). ἐπαίτιοι ‘to blame’ has its verb left out, and so has ἀλλ’ Ἀγαμέμνων; μοι is ‘in my view’. The relative ὅ has σφῶϊ, the dual accusative ‘you two’ (printed with a diaeresis), as its object, and προΐει is the imperfect of προΐημι, as at 326. εἵνεκα ‘for the sake of’ stands inside the phrase Βρισηΐδος … κούρης, ‘the girl Briseis’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε διογενὲς Πατρόκλεες ἔξαγε κούρην
καί σφωϊν δὸς ἄγειν·
sentences.tr:
all’ age diogenes Patroklees exage kourēn
kai sphōïn dos agein·
sentences.l:
But come, Zeus-sprung Patroclus, lead out the girl
and give her to the two of them to lead away;
sentences.i: But come, Zeus-born Patroclus, bring the girl out and give her to them to take away;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε ‘but come’ is the call of 210. διογενές is the stock epithet ‘Zeus-sprung’ of the Odyssey, here in the vocative, a courtesy of address to Patroclus. Πατρόκλεες is the vocative of Πάτροκλος in its fuller form Πατροκλέης. ἔξαγε is the present imperative of ἐξάγω ‘lead out’, σφωϊν the dual dative ‘to the two of them’, and ἄγειν an infinitive of purpose, ‘to lead away’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ αὐτὼ μάρτυροι ἔστων
πρός τε θεῶν μακάρων πρός τε θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων
καὶ πρὸς τοῦ βασιλῆος ἀπηνέος εἴ ποτε δ’ αὖτε
χρειὼ ἐμεῖο γένηται ἀεικέα λοιγὸν ἀμῦναι
τοῖς ἄλλοις·
sentences.tr:
tō d’ autō martyroi estōn
pros te theōn makarōn pros te thnētōn anthrōpōn
kai pros tou basilēos apēneos ei pote d’ aute
chreiō emeio genētai aeikea loigon amynai
tois allois·
sentences.l:
and let those two themselves be witnesses
before the blessed gods and before mortal men
and before that unkind king; and if ever again
there shall be need of me to ward off unseemly ruin
from the others;
sentences.i: and let the two of them be witnesses before the blessed gods, before mortal men, and before that unkind king, if ever again there is need of me to ward off unseemly ruin from the rest;
sentences.n: τὼ … αὐτώ is the dual ‘those two themselves’, the heralds, and ἔστων the dual imperative ‘let them be’; μάρτυροι ‘witnesses’ is followed by πρός with the genitive, ‘in the presence of’. ἀπηνής is ‘unkind’ by the Odyssey’s house rendering, a word for harshness; its origin is not known. The if-clause has no result clause: the threat is left unsaid. χρειώ is ‘need’, with the epic genitive ἐμεῖο ‘of me’; ἀμῦναι is the aorist infinitive of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, with the object ἀεικέα λοιγόν ‘unseemly ruin’ (the Odyssey’s ἀεικής) and the dative τοῖς ἄλλοις ‘for the others’. The same words come at 398.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ ὅ γ’ ὀλοιῇσι φρεσὶ θύει,
οὐδέ τι οἶδε νοῆσαι ἅμα πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω,
ὅππως οἱ παρὰ νηυσὶ σόοι μαχέοιντο Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr:
ē gar ho g’ oloiēisi phresi thyei,
oude ti oide noēsai hama prossō kai opissō,
hoppōs hoi para nēusi sooi macheointo Achaioi.
sentences.i: for he rages with a baleful mind, and does not know how to think at once of what lies ahead and what lies behind: how the Achaeans may fight safely for him beside the ships.”
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ ‘for truly’ gives the reason for what has just been said of Agamemnon. ὀλοιῇσι φρεσί is the dative plural, ‘with baleful wits’ (ὀλοός ‘baleful’), and θύει is the present of θύω ‘rush, rage, seethe’. νοῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of νοέω ‘take thought’, so οἶδε νοῆσαι is ‘knows how to take thought’. ἅμα πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω, ‘at once forward and backward’, is foresight and hindsight, as at Odyssey 24.452. ὅππως (= ὅπως) ‘how’ opens an indirect question with the optative μαχέοιντο; σόοι ‘safe’ is the uncontracted σόος; οἱ ‘for him’, Agamemnon, is a dative of interest. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Πάτροκλος δὲ φίλῳ ἐπεπείθεθ’ ἑταίρῳ,
ἐκ δ’ ἄγαγε κλισίης Βρισηΐδα καλλιπάρῃον,
δῶκε δ’ ἄγειν·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Patroklos de philōi epepeitheth’ hetairōi,
ek d’ agage klisiēs Brisēïda kalliparēion,
dōke d’ agein·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Patroclus obeyed his dear companion, and led Briseis, fair-cheeked, out of the hut, and gave her to them to lead away;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the Odyssey’s ‘So he spoke’. ἐπεπείθεθ’ (= ἐπεπείθετο) is an epic imperfect of πείθομαι ‘obey’, which takes the dative of the person obeyed, φίλῳ ἑταίρῳ, with the final vowel elided. ἐκ … ἄγαγε is a tmesis, ‘led out’, with the genitive κλισίης ‘out of the hut’. δῶκε is the aorist of δίδωμι, and ἄγειν repeats Achilles’ δὸς ἄγειν (338); the receivers are not named.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ αὖτις ἴτην παρὰ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr: tō d’ autis itēn para nēas Achaiōn·
sentences.l: and the two went back again along the ships of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: and the two went back along the ships of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: τὼ is the dual ‘the two’, the heralds; ἴτην is the dual imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’. αὖτις is ‘back, again’, and παρά with the accusative νῆας is ‘along’ the ships.

sentences.t: ἣ δ’ ἀέκουσ’ ἅμα τοῖσι γυνὴ κίεν·
sentences.tr: hē d’ aekous’ hama toisi gynē kien·
sentences.l: and she, unwilling, went along with them, the woman;
sentences.i: and the woman went with them unwilling;
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ is ‘and she’; ἀέκουσ’ is ἀέκουσα, the feminine of the ἀέκοντε said of the heralds at 327, ‘unwilling’. γυνή, ‘woman’, is in apposition to ἥ, and Briseis is not named in the line. κίεν is the unaugmented epic imperfect of κίω ‘go’, and ἅμα ‘along with’ takes the dative τοῖσι, ‘them’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
δακρύσας ἑτάρων ἄφαρ ἕζετο νόσφι λιασθείς,
θῖν’ ἔφ’ ἁλὸς πολιῆς, ὁρόων ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα πόντον·
sentences.tr:
autar Achilleus
dakrysas hetarōn aphar hezeto nosphi liastheis,
thin’ eph’ halos poliēs, horoōn ep’ apeirona ponton·
sentences.i: but Achilles, in tears, withdrew at once from his companions and sat down apart on the shore of the grey sea, looking out over the boundless sea;
sentences.n: δακρύσας is the aorist participle of δακρύω ‘weep’; the aorist says that he broke into tears. ἑτάρων … νόσφι is ‘apart from his companions’, νόσφι taking the genitive; λιασθείς is the aorist passive participle of λιάζομαι ‘withdraw’, and ἄφαρ is ‘at once’. θῖν’ ἔφ’ ἁλὸς πολιῆς is ‘on the shore of the grey sea’: ἔφ’ is ἐπί after its noun, with the π aspirated before the rough breathing of ἁλός. πολιῆς ἁλός ‘grey sea’ is the Odyssey’s phrase, and ἀπείρονα πόντον ‘the boundless open-sea’ uses its ἀπείρων ‘boundless’.

sentences.t: πολλὰ δὲ μητρὶ φίλῃ ἠρήσατο χεῖρας ὀρεγνύς·
sentences.tr: polla de mētri philēi ērēsato cheiras oregnys·
sentences.l: and much to his dear mother he prayed, stretching out his hands;
sentences.i: and he prayed much to his dear mother, stretching out his hands;
sentences.n: πολλά is an adverbial accusative, ‘much, at length’. ἠρήσατο is the aorist of ἀράομαι ‘pray’, with the dative μητρὶ φίλῃ ‘to his dear mother’. ὀρεγνύς is the participle of ὀρέγνυμι, the by-form of ὀρέγω ‘stretch out’; the gesture goes with the prayer.

sentences.t:
μῆτερ ἐπεί μ’ ἔτεκές γε μινυνθάδιόν περ ἐόντα,
τιμήν πέρ μοι ὄφελλεν Ὀλύμπιος ἐγγυαλίξαι
Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης·
sentences.tr:
mēter epei m’ etekes ge minynthadion per eonta,
timēn per moi ophellen Olympios engyalixai
Zeus hypsibremetēs·
sentences.i: “Mother, since you bore me, short-lived as I am, the Olympian, Zeus who thunders on high, ought at least to have granted me honour;
sentences.n: μῆτερ ἐπεί … ἔτεκές γε is ‘since you bore me’, the γε giving the clause its bitter edge. μινυνθάδιον περ ἐόντα is ‘short-lived though I am’ (the Odyssey’s ‘short-lived’), the participle agreeing with μ’; the grievance is that a short life is owed honour. τιμήν … ὄφελλεν ἐγγυαλίξαι: ὄφελλεν is the imperfect of ὀφέλλω ‘ought’, which with an infinitive says what should have happened and did not, ‘ought to have’; ἐγγυαλίξαι is the aorist infinitive of ἐγγυαλίζω ‘put into the hands, grant’. Ὀλύμπιος is the adjective ‘Olympian’, and ὑψιβρεμέτης is the Odyssey’s ‘who thunders on high’.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ οὐδέ με τυτθὸν ἔτισεν·
sentences.tr: nyn d’ oude me tytthon etisen·
sentences.l: but now not even a little has he honoured me;
sentences.i: but as it is, he has not honoured me even a little;
sentences.n: νῦν δέ is ‘but as it is’, the real state of things set against the wish. τυτθόν ‘a little’ is an adverbial accusative. ἔτισεν is the aorist of τίω ‘honour’, the verb belonging with the noun τιμήν of the line before.

sentences.t:
ἦ γάρ μ’ Ἀτρεΐδης εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
ἠτίμησεν·
sentences.tr:
ē gar m’ Atreïdēs eury kreiōn Agamemnōn
ētimēsen·
sentences.l:
for truly me Atreus’-son, wide-ruling Agamemnon,
dishonoured;
sentences.i: for the son of Atreus, wide-ruling Agamemnon, has dishonoured me;
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ ‘for truly’ gives the proof of what he has just said. εὐρὺ κρείων is printed as two words; εὐρύ is the adverb ‘widely’ and κρείων ‘ruling’, so ‘wide-ruling’, the house rendering. ἠτίμησεν is the aorist of ἀτιμάω ‘dishonour’, the opposite of τίω; Calchas used this verb of Agamemnon’s treatment of Chryses at 1.94.

sentences.t: ἑλὼν γὰρ ἔχει γέρας αὐτὸς ἀπούρας.
sentences.tr: helōn gar echei geras autos apouras.
sentences.l: for he has taken and holds the prize, himself having taken it away.”
sentences.i: for he has taken my prize of honour and keeps it, having seized it himself.”
sentences.n: ἑλὼν ἔχει, ‘having taken he holds’, is a way of saying ‘has taken and keeps’. γέρας is the prize of honour, here Briseis, and the English is the same at every occurrence (‘prize’ in the literal line, ‘prize of honour’ in the free English). αὐτός ‘himself’ stresses that Agamemnon did it in person. ἀπούρας is the aorist participle of the old verb ἀπαυράω ‘take away from’, as in the Odyssey’s θυμὸν ἀπούρας ‘having taken his life’; the person robbed, ‘me’, is left unsaid. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο δάκρυ χέων, τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε πότνια μήτηρ
ἡμένη ἐν βένθεσσιν ἁλὸς παρὰ πατρὶ γέροντι·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato dakry cheōn, tou d’ eklye potnia mētēr
hēmenē en benthessin halos para patri geronti·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, a tear shedding, and him heard his lady mother
sitting in the depths of the sea beside her old father;
sentences.i: So he spoke, shedding tears, and his lady mother heard him as she sat in the depths of the sea beside her old father;
sentences.n: τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε ‘and him heard’: κλύω takes the genitive of the one heard, as in the prayer-closing lines of the Odyssey. δάκρυ χέων, ‘shedding a tear’, is the Odyssey’s phrase. πότνια μήτηρ is ‘lady mother’, πότνια the feminine of the title ‘lady’. She is Thetis, but the Greek does not name her yet, nor her father, the old man of the sea; ἡμένη ‘sitting’, ἐν βένθεσσιν, the epic dative plural of βένθος ‘depth’, ἁλός ‘of the sea’.

sentences.t:
καρπαλίμως δ’ ἀνέδυ πολιῆς ἁλὸς ἠΰτ’ ὀμίχλη,
καί ῥα πάροιθ’ αὐτοῖο καθέζετο δάκρυ χέοντος,
χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr:
karpalimōs d’ anedy poliēs halos ēÿt’ omichlē,
kai rha paroith’ autoio kathezeto dakry cheontos,
cheiri te min katerexen epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l:
And swiftly she rose up out of the grey sea like a mist,
and then before him sat down, as he a tear shed,
and stroked him with her hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: She rose up swiftly out of the grey sea like a mist, and sat down before him as he shed tears, and stroked him with her hand, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: καρπαλίμως is ‘swiftly’. ἀνέδυ is the aorist of ἀναδύομαι ‘rise up out of’ and takes the genitive πολιῆς ἁλός ‘out of the grey sea’. ἠΰτ’ ὀμίχλη, ‘like a mist’, uses the Odyssey’s ‘like’ for ἠΰτε. καί ῥα is ‘and then’. αὐτοῖο is the epic genitive of αὐτός, ‘him’, agreeing with the participle δάκρυ χέοντος ‘as he shed a tear’. The last line is the Odyssey’s formula of stroking and address, in the same English, with ‘her’ for a female subject (Odyssey 4.610; of a goddess, 5.181).

sentences.t: τέκνον τί κλαίεις;
sentences.tr: teknon ti klaieis;
sentences.l: “Child, why do you weep?
sentences.i: “Child, why are you weeping?
sentences.n: τέκνον is ‘child’, the form of address. τί is the neuter of the interrogative used as an adverb, ‘why’, and κλαίεις is the present of κλαίω ‘weep’. The edition ends the question with its Greek question mark, a semicolon.

sentences.t: τί δέ σε φρένας ἵκετο πένθος;
sentences.tr: ti de se phrenas hiketo penthos;
sentences.l: And what grief has come to your wits?
sentences.i: And what grief has come over your mind?
sentences.n: τί … πένθος is ‘what grief’, with τί as an adjective. σε φρένας is the ‘whole and part’ construction, ‘you, in your wits’, both accusatives with ἵκετο, the unaugmented aorist of ἵκομαι ‘come to’.

sentences.t: ἐξαύδα, μὴ κεῦθε νόῳ, ἵνα εἴδομεν ἄμφω.
sentences.tr: exauda, mē keuthe noōi, hina eidomen amphō.
sentences.l: Speak out, do not hide it in your mind, so that we may both know.”
sentences.i: Speak it out, do not keep it hidden in your mind, so that we may both know.”
sentences.n: ἐξαύδα is the imperative of ἐξαυδάω ‘speak out’. μὴ κεῦθε forbids with the present imperative of κεύθω ‘hide’, and νόῳ is the dative of νόος ‘mind’. ἵνα εἴδομεν is ἵνα with the epic short-vowel subjunctive of οἶδα, εἴδομεν for εἰδῶμεν, ‘that we may know’. ἄμφω ‘both’ means she and he together.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ βαρὺ στενάχων προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn de bary stenachōn prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Her, groaning heavily, addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: Groaning heavily, Achilles, swift of foot, said to her:
sentences.n: τὴν is the article used as a pronoun, ‘her’, Thetis. βαρὺ στενάχων is ‘groaning heavily’, βαρύ being a neuter accusative used as an adverb (the Odyssey has the plural βαρέα στενάχοντα). The line is the reply-formula of the Odyssey, τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη, with ‘groaning heavily’ in place of ‘answering’. πόδας ὠκύς is the stock epithet, ‘swift-in-feet’ in the literal line, ‘swift of foot’ in the free English.

sentences.t: οἶσθα·
sentences.tr: oistha·
sentences.l: “You know;
sentences.i: “You know.
sentences.n: οἶσθα is the second person singular of οἶδα ‘know’, a perfect with present sense. The edition sets a high stop after it, so the word stands as a sentence of its own: she knows already.

sentences.t: τί ἤ τοι ταῦτα ἰδυίῃ πάντ’ ἀγορεύω;
sentences.tr: ti ē toi tauta iduiēi pant’ agoreuō;
sentences.l: why indeed to you, knowing these things, do I tell it all?
sentences.i: Why should I tell it all to you, who know it already?
sentences.n: ἤ τοι is printed as two words: ἤ is the particle ἦ ‘indeed’, and τοι is to be taken as σοι ‘to you’, since ἰδυίῃ, the dative feminine singular of the perfect participle of οἶδα, ‘knowing’, needs a dative to agree with: ‘to you, who know these things’. ἀγορεύω is ‘speak out, tell’; the present is a question of deliberation, ‘why am I to tell?’. ταῦτα … πάντ’ is ‘all these things’.

sentences.t:
ᾠχόμεθ’ ἐς Θήβην ἱερὴν πόλιν Ἠετίωνος,
τὴν δὲ διεπράθομέν τε καὶ ἤγομεν ἐνθάδε πάντα·
sentences.tr:
ōichometh’ es Thēbēn hierēn polin Ēetiōnos,
tēn de dieprathomen te kai ēgomen enthade panta·
sentences.l:
We went to Thebe, the sacred city of Eëtion,
and that we sacked, and brought here everything;
sentences.i: We went to Thebe, the sacred city of Eëtion, and sacked it, and brought everything here;
sentences.n: ᾠχόμεθ’ is ᾠχόμεθα, the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go off’. This Thebe is the city of Eëtion, not Boeotian Thebes. The Greek says only that it was sacked and its spoil brought to the camp. ἱερήν ‘sacred’ is the usual adjective for a city. διεπράθομεν is the aorist of διαπέρθω ‘sack utterly’, ‘sacked’ as in the Odyssey, and ἤγομεν is the imperfect of ἄγω ‘lead, carry off’, used of spoil. τὴν δέ puts the city first for emphasis.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν εὖ δάσσαντο μετὰ σφίσιν υἷες Ἀχαιῶν,
ἐκ δ’ ἕλον Ἀτρεΐδῃ Χρυσηΐδα καλλιπάρῃον.
sentences.tr:
kai ta men eu dassanto meta sphisin huies Achaiōn,
ek d’ helon Atreïdēi Chrysēïda kalliparēion.
sentences.l:
And these things the sons of the Achaeans divided well among themselves,
and picked out for Atreus’-son Chryseis, fair-cheeked.
sentences.i: The sons of the Achaeans divided the spoil well among themselves, and picked out Chryseis, fair-cheeked, for the son of Atreus.
sentences.n: τὰ μέν, ‘these things’, the spoil, is set against ἐκ δ’ ἕλον, ‘but they picked out’: the ordinary shares were divided, and one prize chosen apart for the king. δάσσαντο is the aorist middle of δατέομαι ‘divide among themselves’, and σφίσιν ‘among themselves’ repeats the middle. ἐκ … ἕλον is a tmesis, ‘picked out’, with the dative Ἀτρεΐδῃ ‘for the son of Atreus’. Chryseis has the same epithet, καλλιπάρῃος ‘fair-cheeked’, that Briseis has at 323.

sentences.t:
Χρύσης δ’ αὖθ’ ἱερεὺς ἑκατηβόλου Ἀπόλλωνος
ἦλθε θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
λυσόμενός τε θύγατρα φέρων τ’ ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα,
sentences.tr:
Chrysēs d’ auth’ hiereus hekatēbolou Apollōnos
ēlthe thoas epi nēas Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn
lysomenos te thygatra pherōn t’ apereisi’ apoina,
sentences.l:
And Chryses, in turn, priest of far-shooting Apollo,
came to the swift ships of the bronze-shirted Achaeans
to ransom his daughter and bringing unstinted ransom,
sentences.i: Then Chryses, priest of Apollo who shoots from afar, came to the swift ships of the bronze-shirted Achaeans to win back his daughter, bringing an unstinted ransom,
sentences.n: Achilles now tells Thetis the story from its start, which the reader knows from 1.11; αὖθ’ (= αὖτε) marks the next step. ἑκατηβόλου keeps the Odyssey’s ‘far-shooting’ in the literal line and ‘who shoots from afar’ in the free English; at 373 ἑκηβόλου is the same epithet in a shorter form, with the English already given it in this poem, ‘far-shooting’. χαλκοχιτώνων is the Odyssey’s ‘bronze-shirted’. λυσόμενος is the future participle of purpose, ‘to ransom’, and ἀπερείσι’ is ἀπερείσια ‘unstinted’, elided. Lines 372–375 repeat 1.13–16 word for word, and 371 is 1.12 without ὃ γάρ and with χαλκοχιτώνων added, so the English follows 1.12–16.

sentences.t:
στέμματ’ ἔχων ἐν χερσὶν ἑκηβόλου Ἀπόλλωνος
χρυσέῳ ἀνὰ σκήπτρῳ, καὶ λίσσετο πάντας Ἀχαιούς,
Ἀτρεΐδα δὲ μάλιστα δύω κοσμήτορε λαῶν.
sentences.tr:
stemmat’ echōn en chersin hekēbolou Apollōnos
chryseōi ana skēptrōi, kai lisseto pantas Achaious,
Atreïda de malista dyō kosmētore laōn.
sentences.l:
the fillets holding in his hands of far-shooting Apollo
upon a golden sceptre, and he begged all the Achaeans,
but most of all the two sons of Atreus, the two marshallers of the people.
sentences.i: with the fillets of far-shooting Apollo in his hands on a golden sceptre; and he begged all the Achaeans, and most of all the two sons of Atreus, marshals of the people.
sentences.n: στέμματ’ ἔχων is ‘holding the fillets’, those of the god, on a golden sceptre; λίσσετο is the imperfect of λίσσομαι ‘beg’. Ἀτρεΐδα and κοσμήτορε are duals, the two sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus, and the Greek does not name them here. The sense runs on from 372, as one sentence of six lines, which the translation cuts at the comma after ἄποινα (372) to keep each unit short.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι μὲν πάντες ἐπευφήμησαν Ἀχαιοὶ
αἰδεῖσθαί θ’ ἱερῆα καὶ ἀγλαὰ δέχθαι ἄποινα·
sentences.tr:
enth’ alloi men pantes epeuphēmēsan Achaioi
aideisthai th’ hierēa kai aglaa dechthai apoina·
sentences.l:
Then all the other Achaeans shouted-assent,
to respect the priest and to accept the splendid ransom;
sentences.i: Then all the other Achaeans cried out in favour of respecting the priest and accepting the splendid ransom;
sentences.n: These two lines are 1.22–23 word for word, in the same English. ἐπευφήμησαν, from ἐπευφημέω, is to voice assent aloud; the infinitives αἰδεῖσθαι ‘to respect’ and δέχθαι ‘to accept’ say what they called for. δέχθαι is an athematic aorist infinitive of δέχομαι. ἱερῆα is the epic accusative of ἱερεύς ‘priest’, and ἀγλαά ‘splendid’ is the house rendering of ἀγλαός.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι ἥνδανε θυμῷ,
ἀλλὰ κακῶς ἀφίει, κρατερὸν δ’ ἐπὶ μῦθον ἔτελλε·
sentences.tr:
all’ ouk Atreïdēi Agamemnoni hēndane thymōi,
alla kakōs aphiei, krateron d’ epi mython etelle·
sentences.l:
but not to Atreus’ son Agamemnon was it pleasing in his heart,
but harshly he sent him away, and a strong word enjoined on him:
sentences.i: but it did not please the heart of Agamemnon, son of Atreus: he sent him off harshly and laid a strong charge on him.
sentences.n: These two lines are 1.24–25 word for word, in the same English. ἥνδανε θυμῷ is ‘was pleasing to his heart’, with Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι the dative of the person. ἀφίει is the unaugmented imperfect of ἀφίημι ‘send away’. ἐπὶ … ἔτελλε is the tmesis met at 326, ‘laid a charge on’.

sentences.t: χωόμενος δ’ ὁ γέρων πάλιν ᾤχετο·
sentences.tr: chōomenos d’ ho gerōn palin ōicheto·
sentences.l: And, incensed, the old man went back;
sentences.i: Incensed, the old man went back;
sentences.n: χωόμενος is the participle of χώομαι ‘be incensed’, as in χωόμενος κῆρ at 1.44. ὁ γέρων is ‘the old man’, Achilles’ name for Chryses, a figure the poem has already introduced. πάλιν is ‘back’, and ᾤχετο the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘went off’.

sentences.t:
τοῖο δ’ Ἀπόλλων
εὐξαμένου ἤκουσεν, ἐπεὶ μάλα οἱ φίλος ἦεν,
ἧκε δ’ ἐπ’ Ἀργείοισι κακὸν βέλος·
sentences.tr:
toio d’ Apollōn
euxamenou ēkousen, epei mala hoi philos ēen,
hēke d’ ep’ Argeioisi kakon belos·
sentences.i: and Apollo heard him when he prayed, since he was very dear to him, and sent an evil shaft against the Argives;
sentences.n: τοῖο is the epic genitive of τοῦ, ‘him’, the old man; it goes with εὐξαμένου, the aorist participle of εὔχομαι ‘pray’ (‘of him praying’), since ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person heard. ἦεν is ἦν ‘was’; the one who was dear is Chryses, and οἱ ‘to him’ is Apollo. ἧκε is the aorist of ἵημι ‘send, shoot’, and ἐπ’ Ἀργείοισι is ‘upon the Argives’. The Iliad keeps the army’s three names, Achaeans, Danaans and Argives, in English as the poet gives them. βέλος ‘shaft’ is the plague.

sentences.t:
οἳ δέ νυ λαοὶ
θνῇσκον ἐπασσύτεροι, τὰ δ’ ἐπῴχετο κῆλα θεοῖο
πάντῃ ἀνὰ στρατὸν εὐρὺν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr:
hoi de ny laoi
thnēiskon epassyteroi, ta d’ epōicheto kēla theoio
pantēi ana straton euryn Achaiōn·
sentences.i: and the people died one close upon another, and the god’s shafts went about everywhere through the wide army of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ νυ λαοί is ‘and those people’, the relative form used as a demonstrative, with νυ the particle ‘now, then’. θνῇσκον is the unaugmented imperfect of θνῄσκω ‘die’. ἐπασσύτεροι has the form of a comparative and means ‘one close upon another’; that sense is the traditional one. τὰ δ’ ἐπῴχετο κῆλα θεοῖο is ‘and the shafts of the god went about’, ἐπῴχετο being the imperfect of ἐποίχομαι. κῆλα θεοῖο keeps the table’s ‘the god’s shafts’. πάντῃ is ‘everywhere’, and ἀνὰ στρατὸν εὐρύν ‘through the wide army’ (ἀνά ‘up and down’).

sentences.t:
ἄμμι δὲ μάντις
εὖ εἰδὼς ἀγόρευε θεοπροπίας ἑκάτοιο.
sentences.tr:
ammi de mantis
eu eidōs agoreue theopropias hekatoio.
sentences.l:
and to us a seer
who knew well declared the prophecies of the far-darter.
sentences.i: and a seer who knew well declared to us the prophecies of the far-darter.
sentences.n: ἄμμι is the Aeolic dative ‘to us’ (= ἡμῖν). The seer is Calchas, unnamed here. εὖ εἰδώς is ‘knowing well’, the participle of οἶδα, and what he knows is not stated. ἀγόρευε is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω ‘speak out’, a public declaration here. θεοπροπίας is ‘prophecies’, and ἑκάτοιο the genitive of ἕκατος, a short form of the god’s epithet, probably the same word as in ἑκατηβόλος and ἑκατηβελέτης, so ‘far-darter’ is the English of that family; its exact sense is not certain.

sentences.t: αὐτίκ’ ἐγὼ πρῶτος κελόμην θεὸν ἱλάσκεσθαι·
sentences.tr: autik’ egō prōtos kelomēn theon hilaskesthai·
sentences.l: At once I first urged to appease the god;
sentences.i: At once I was the first to urge that the god be appeased;
sentences.n: αὐτίκα is ‘at once’, and πρῶτος ‘first’ agrees with ἐγώ. κελόμην is the unaugmented imperfect of κέλομαι ‘urge, bid’, used as a narrative past, with an infinitive; the people urged are not named. ἱλάσκεσθαι is the infinitive of ἱλάσκομαι ‘appease’, with θεόν as its object. This is Achilles’ own account of who spoke first.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐωνα δ’ ἔπειτα χόλος λάβεν, αἶψα δ’ ἀναστὰς
ἠπείλησεν μῦθον ὃ δὴ τετελεσμένος ἐστί·
sentences.tr:
Atreïōna d’ epeita cholos laben, aipsa d’ anastas
ēpeilēsen mython ho dē tetelesmenos esti·
sentences.l:
But Atreus’-son then anger seized, and at once, rising,
he threatened a word that has indeed been fulfilled;
sentences.i: Then anger seized the son of Atreus, and, standing up at once, he uttered a threat, a word that has now been fulfilled;
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐωνα is the patronymic in -ίων, a variant of Ἀτρεΐδης, the same man; he is the object of λάβεν, the unaugmented aorist of λαμβάνω ‘seize’, with χόλος ‘anger’ as subject. ἀναστάς is the aorist participle of ἀνίστημι, and αἶψα ‘at once’. ἠπείλησεν μῦθον is ‘threatened a word’: the threat is the word. In ὃ δὴ τετελεσμένος ἐστί the relative ὅ is neuter but τετελεσμένος, the perfect passive participle of τελέω ‘fulfil’, is masculine like μῦθον, a loose agreement. The sense is that the threat has come true now that the heralds have gone for Briseis.

sentences.t:
τὴν μὲν γὰρ σὺν νηῒ θοῇ ἑλίκωπες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἐς Χρύσην πέμπουσιν, ἄγουσι δὲ δῶρα ἄνακτι·
sentences.tr:
tēn men gar syn nēï thoēi helikōpes Achaioi
es Chrysēn pempousin, agousi de dōra anakti·
sentences.l:
For her, with a swift ship, the quick-eyed Achaeans
send to Chryse, and they bring gifts to the lord;
sentences.i: For the quick-eyed Achaeans are sending her to Chryse on a swift ship, and taking gifts for the lord;
sentences.n: τὴν μὲν … is set against τὴν δέ of the next line: Chryseis goes, Briseis is taken. γάρ gives the reason for the fulfilment just claimed. πέμπουσιν and ἄγουσι are presents for what is going on now, the ship of 308–311 being under way. ἑλίκωπες is the masculine plural of ἑλίκωψ, the word that gives ἑλικῶπις of women; its sense is disputed, and ‘quick-eyed’ is one traditional explanation. ἐς Χρύσην is ‘to Chryse’, the place. ἄνακτι ‘to the lord’ is Apollo.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ νέον κλισίηθεν ἔβαν κήρυκες ἄγοντες
κούρην Βρισῆος τήν μοι δόσαν υἷες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
tēn de neon klisiēthen eban kērykes agontes
kourēn Brisēos tēn moi dosan huies Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
but her, just now, from the hut went heralds, leading,
the girl of Briseus, whom to me gave the sons of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: but just now the heralds have gone from the hut, leading away the girl, the daughter of Briseus, whom the sons of the Achaeans gave me.
sentences.n: τὴν δὲ … κούρην is Briseis, ‘the girl’ standing in apposition; Βρισηΐς is made from Βρισεύς and means ‘daughter of Briseus’. νέον is ‘newly, just now’, κλισίηθεν ‘from the hut’ (with -θεν), and ἔβαν = ἔβησαν ‘went’. κήρυκες is the plural, though the pair was dual at 321. δόσαν is the unaugmented ἔδοσαν ‘gave’, and the army’s gift is the γέρας of 356; υἷες Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the sons of the Achaeans’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ σὺ εἰ δύνασαί γε περίσχεο παιδὸς ἑῆος·
sentences.tr: alla sy ei dynasai ge perischeo paidos heēos·
sentences.l: But you, if you are able, protect your own son;
sentences.i: But if you are able, you must protect your own son;
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ σὺ εἰ δύνασαί γε is ‘but you, if you at least are able’, with γε limiting the condition. περίσχεο is the aorist imperative middle of περιέχω; with the genitive παιδός it means ‘protect’. ἑῆος is taken as ‘one’s own’ (ἑός, the possessive met at 333), though the form is also read as the genitive of ἐΰς ‘good’.

sentences.t:
ἐλθοῦσ’ Οὔλυμπον δὲ Δία λίσαι, εἴ ποτε δή τι
ἢ ἔπει ὤνησας κραδίην Διὸς ἠὲ καὶ ἔργῳ.
sentences.tr:
elthous’ Oulympon de Dia lisai, ei pote dē ti
ē epei ōnēsas kradiēn Dios ēe kai ergōi.
sentences.l:
having gone to Olympus, beg Zeus, if ever at all
either by a word you helped the heart of Zeus or even by a deed.
sentences.i: Go to Olympus and beg Zeus, if ever you helped the heart of Zeus at all, whether by word or by deed.
sentences.n: ἐλθοῦσ’ is the aorist participle ‘having gone’, which carries an order alongside the imperative λίσαι. Οὔλυμπον δέ is Οὔλυμπον with the suffix -δε ‘to’; Οὔλυμπος is Ὄλυμπος with the first vowel lengthened for the verse. Δία is the accusative of Ζεύς, and λίσαι the aorist imperative of λίσσομαι ‘beg’ (as in λίσσετο at 374). εἴ ποτε δή τι is ‘if ever at all’. ὤνησας is the aorist of ὀνίνημι ‘help, benefit’, with κραδίην Διός as its object; ἔπει is the dative of ἔπος ‘by a word’, ἔργῳ ‘by a deed’, and ἢ … ἠὲ καὶ is ‘either … or even’.

sentences.t:
πολλάκι γάρ σεο πατρὸς ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἄκουσα
εὐχομένης ὅτ’ ἔφησθα κελαινεφέϊ Κρονίωνι
οἴη ἐν ἀθανάτοισιν ἀεικέα λοιγὸν ἀμῦναι,
sentences.tr:
pollaki gar seo patros eni megaroisin akousa
euchomenēs hot’ ephēstha kelainepheï Kroniōni
oiē en athanatoisin aeikea loigon amynai,
sentences.l:
For many a time in the halls of your father I heard
you boasting, when you said that to the dark-clouded son of Cronus
you alone among the immortals warded off unseemly ruin,
sentences.i: For I have often heard you in your father’s halls, boasting that you alone among the immortals once warded off unseemly ruin from the son of Cronus of the dark clouds,
sentences.n: πολλάκι is πολλάκις ‘many times’. σεο is the epic genitive of σύ; ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person with a participle, εὐχομένης ‘you boasting’. εὔχομαι is ‘boast, claim’ here (the same verb also means ‘pray’), and ἔφησθα is the second person imperfect of φημί ‘say’. The infinitive ἀμῦναι is indirect speech after it, ‘you said you warded off’, and the dative κελαινεφέϊ Κρονίωνι is the one helped; the words ἀεικέα λοιγὸν ἀμῦναι are those of 341. κελαινεφής is ‘dark-clouded’ (κελαινός ‘black’, νέφος ‘cloud’). οἴη is ‘alone’, agreeing with a σύ left unsaid. The father’s halls are those of the old man at 358.

sentences.t:
ὁππότε μιν ξυνδῆσαι Ὀλύμπιοι ἤθελον ἄλλοι
Ἥρη τ’ ἠδὲ Ποσειδάων καὶ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr:
hoppote min xyndēsai Olympioi ēthelon alloi
Hērē t’ ēde Poseidaōn kai Pallas Athēnē·
sentences.l:
when him to bind together the Olympians wished, the others,
Hera and Poseidon and Pallas Athena;
sentences.i: when the other Olympians wished to bind him, Hera and Poseidon and Pallas Athena;
sentences.n: ὁππότε is ὁπότε ‘when’, with the doubled π needed by the verse. μιν is Zeus. ξυνδῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of συνδέω ‘bind together, bind fast’, and ἤθελον ‘wished’ is an imperfect. Ὀλύμπιοι ἄλλοι is ‘the other Olympians’, those other than Zeus, who is Ὀλύμπιος himself at 353; the three are named in apposition. The Greek tells no more of this story here.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ τόν γ’ ἐλθοῦσα θεὰ ὑπελύσαο δεσμῶν,
ὦχ’ ἑκατόγχειρον καλέσασ’ ἐς μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον,
ὃν Βριάρεων καλέουσι θεοί, ἄνδρες δέ τε πάντες
Αἰγαίων’, ὃ γὰρ αὖτε βίην οὗ πατρὸς ἀμείνων·
sentences.tr:
alla sy ton g’ elthousa thea hypelysao desmōn,
ōch’ hekatoncheiron kalesas’ es makron Olympon,
hon Briareōn kaleousi theoi, andres de te pantes
Aigaiōn’, ho gar aute biēn hou patros ameinōn·
sentences.l:
But you, him, having come, goddess, set free from his bonds,
quickly, the hundred-handed one summoning to tall Olympus,
whom Briareus the gods call, but all men
Aegaeon, for he in turn in might than his father is better;
sentences.i: But you, goddess, went and set him free from his bonds, quickly summoning the hundred-handed one to tall Olympus, whom the gods call Briareus, but all men Aegaeon, for he in his turn is better in might than his father;
sentences.n: ὑπελύσαο is the aorist middle of ὑπολύω ‘loose from under’, with the genitive δεσμῶν ‘from his bonds’; τόν γε is Zeus, and θεά the vocative. ὦχ’ is ὦκα ‘quickly’, changed before the rough breathing of ἑκατόγχειρον ‘hundred-handed’ (ἑκατόν, χείρ). ἐς μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον is the Odyssey’s ‘to tall Olympus’. ὃν Βριάρεων καλέουσι θεοί is the gods’ name and ἄνδρες δέ τε πάντες Αἰγαίων’ (Αἰγαίωνα, elided) the men’s, the verb left unsaid. In ὃ γὰρ αὖτε βίην οὗ πατρὸς ἀμείνων, οὗ is the possessive ‘his own’, βίην an accusative of respect ‘in might’, and πατρός the genitive of comparison after ἀμείνων; the father is not named.

sentences.t: ὅς ῥα παρὰ Κρονίωνι καθέζετο κύδεϊ γαίων·
sentences.tr: hos rha para Kroniōni kathezeto kydeï gaiōn·
sentences.l: who then beside the son of Cronus sat down, exulting in glory;
sentences.i: who sat down beside the son of Cronus, exulting in his glory;
sentences.n: ὅς ῥα is ‘who then’. Κρονίωνι, ‘the son of Cronus’, is Zeus, so that the hundred-handed one took his seat at Zeus’s side. καθέζετο is ‘sat down’. γαίων is the participle of γαίω ‘exult, be proud’, with the dative κύδεϊ ‘in glory’; κῦδος is the glory that goes with success.

sentences.t: τὸν καὶ ὑπέδεισαν μάκαρες θεοὶ οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἔδησαν.
sentences.tr: ton kai hypedeisan makares theoi oud’ et’ edēsan.
sentences.l: him even the blessed gods feared, and no longer bound;
sentences.i: and even the blessed gods were afraid of him, and did not go on to bind Zeus.
sentences.n: τὸν is Briareus, and καί ‘even’. ὑπέδεισαν is the aorist of ὑποδείδω ‘shrink in fear from’; μάκαρες ‘blessed’. οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἔδησαν is ‘and no longer bound’: the verb has no object in the Greek, and the one meant is Zeus, the μιν of 399. The line says the gods gave up the binding; whether they had begun it the Greek does not say. ἔδησαν is the aorist of δέω ‘bind’.

sentences.t:
τῶν νῦν μιν μνήσασα παρέζεο καὶ λαβὲ γούνων
αἴ κέν πως ἐθέλῃσιν ἐπὶ Τρώεσσιν ἀρῆξαι,
τοὺς δὲ κατὰ πρύμνας τε καὶ ἀμφ’ ἅλα ἔλσαι Ἀχαιοὺς
κτεινομένους, ἵνα πάντες ἐπαύρωνται βασιλῆος,
sentences.tr:
tōn nyn min mnēsasa parezeo kai labe gounōn
ai ken pōs ethelēisin epi Trōessin arēxai,
tous de kata prymnas te kai amph’ hala elsai Achaious
kteinomenous, hina pantes epaurōntai basilēos,
sentences.l:
Of these things now having reminded him, sit beside him, and take hold of his knees,
if in some way he may be willing to help the Trojans,
but those Achaeans at the sterns and around the salt-sea to hem in,
being killed, so that all may have the benefit of their king,
sentences.i: Remind him of this now, sit beside him and take hold of his knees, in case he will be willing to help the Trojans and to hem the Achaeans in at the sterns and around the salt sea as they are killed, so that all of them may have the benefit of their king,
sentences.n: τῶν is the genitive after μνήσασα ‘having reminded’, a participle used like an imperative beside παρέζεο ‘sit down beside’ and λαβὲ γούνων ‘take hold of his knees’ (genitive of the part grasped): the posture of a suppliant. αἴ κέν πως ἐθέλῃσιν is ‘in case he may be willing’; ἀρῆξαι ‘to help’ goes with ἐπὶ Τρώεσσιν ‘in aid of the Trojans’, and τοὺς … Ἀχαιούς is the object of ἔλσαι, ‘to hem in’ (εἴλω). ἐπαύρωνται is the aorist subjunctive of ἐπαυρίσκομαι ‘get, enjoy’, with the genitive; the verb often means getting the result of something, good or bad, so the line is bitter.

sentences.t:
γνῷ δὲ καὶ Ἀτρεΐδης εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
ἣν ἄτην ὅ τ’ ἄριστον Ἀχαιῶν οὐδὲν ἔτισεν.
sentences.tr:
gnōi de kai Atreïdēs eury kreiōn Agamemnōn
hēn atēn ho t’ ariston Achaiōn ouden etisen.
sentences.l:
and may know also Atreus’-son, wide-ruling Agamemnon,
his own bewilderment, that the best of the Achaeans he honoured not at all.”
sentences.i: and so that Agamemnon, wide-ruling son of Atreus, may know his own bewilderment, that he paid no honour at all to the best of the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: γνῷ is the aorist subjunctive of γιγνώσκω in the purpose clause begun by ἵνα at 410, and the δέ adds a second purpose to the first. ἣν is the possessive ‘his own’, and ἄτη is ‘bewilderment’, as in the Odyssey: the clouding of the mind that brings ruin. ὅ τ’ (= ὅ τε) is ‘that’ and gives the content of the ἄτη, Agamemnon’s failure to honour Achilles. The second half of the line is Achilles’ own at 244 (there ἔτισας, second person), and the English is the same with the person changed. εὐρὺ κρείων is ‘wide-ruling’ as at 355. The speech ends here.
